posts.title: The uncomfortable truth about AI-assisted development
posts.body:
I've built 26 tools with Claude Code.

Here's what I don't tell people:

I have no idea how most of them work internally.

And I'm okay with that.

The traditional view: 'You must understand every line of code you ship.'

My reality:

I understand:
- What problem it solves
- What inputs it takes
- What outputs it produces
- How to test it works
- How to iterate when it doesn't

I don't understand:
- The specific syntax
- Library internals
- Optimization choices

Why this works:

My tools are personal productivity tools.
Not production systems for millions of users.
Not safety-critical applications.
Not financial infrastructure.

Context matters.

For my use case:
- Speed of building > perfect understanding
- Solving problems > writing elegant code
- Shipping > studying

How I validate without understanding:

1. Define expected behavior clearly
2. Test with real inputs
3. Check edge cases
4. Verify outputs match expectations
5. If it works correctly, it works

The caveat:

This approach is for personal tools and MVPs.

Production systems at scale? Different conversation.

Takeaway: Enough understanding to verify it works, debug when it breaks, and iterate to improvement. That's all you need for most use cases. Know your context.
posts.cta: Where do you draw the line on 'necessary understanding'?

posts.title: How to build your first AI agent (even if you've never coded)
posts.body:
'Agent' sounds intimidating.

It doesn't have to be.

An agent is just: AI + tools + memory + decision-making.

Here's how I built my first one:

Step 1: Define one specific job

Not 'help me with stuff.'

Specific: 'Categorize my incoming ideas and add them to my backlog.'

One job. One outcome.

Step 2: Give it tools

Tools are just things it can do:
- Read a file
- Write to a database
- Send a message
- Call an API

My first agent had 3 tools:
- Read incoming message
- Categorize content
- Append to backlog file

Step 3: Add memory

Memory = context that persists.

For my agent:
- My project categories
- My priority criteria
- My formatting preferences

Stored in a simple JSON file that gets loaded each time.

Step 4: Define decision rules

How should it decide what to do?

My rules:
- If message contains project idea -> categorize as 'development'
- If message mentions content -> categorize as 'content'
- If unclear -> categorize as 'research'
- Always add to backlog with timestamp

Step 5: Test with real inputs

Sent it 10 real ideas.
Checked categorization accuracy.
Refined rules based on mistakes.

The Result:

A working agent that:
- Receives my ideas (via Telegram)
- Categorizes automatically
- Adds to my backlog
- Never forgets anything

Time to build: One afternoon.

Takeaway: Agents aren't magic. They're AI with a specific job, tools to do that job, memory to do it consistently, and rules for decision-making. Start simple. Add complexity later.
posts.cta: What repetitive task would you give to your first agent?

DMs from lurkers.
Conversations at events.

100 posts with 10 likes each = 1,000 touchpoints.

3. Don't check metrics for 30 days
4. Focus on the building, not the likes

posts.title: The debugging mindset that makes AI coding actually work
posts.body:
Most people give up when Claude's code doesn't work.

I've learned to expect it.

The mindset shift:

First attempt rarely works. That's NORMAL.

Errors aren't failures. They're information.

My debugging workflow:

Step 1: Run it immediately

Don't try to understand the code first.
Run it. See what happens.

Step 2: Capture the EXACT error

No paraphrasing. No summarizing.
Copy the entire error message.
Include the full stack trace.

Step 3: Share everything with Claude

'Here's the error I got: [paste full error]'

Claude can debug with full context.

Step 4: Test the fix immediately

Don't wait. Run it again.
New error? Back to step 2.
It works? Move to the next feature.

Step 5: Budget for iterations

- Simple features: 2-3 iterations
- Medium features: 4-5 iterations
- Complex features: 5-10 iterations

This is NORMAL. Plan for it.

Common error patterns I've learned:

'Module not found' -> Install the dependency (pip install X)
'Undefined variable' -> Check spelling or scope
'Type error' -> Data format mismatch
'Connection refused' -> Service not running

Most errors are simple once you've seen them a few times.

How to build this mindset:

1. Expect 3-5 iterations for any feature
2. Never paraphrase errors
3. Celebrate fixed bugs, not first-try successes
4. Keep a log of errors you've solved

Takeaway: Debugging is a skill. You get better with practice. Each error you fix teaches you patterns. Week 1: Panic at every error. Week 8: Debug most issues in under 5 minutes.
posts.cta: What's your debugging process when AI code doesn't work?

posts.title: The data processing architecture I use for every project
posts.body:
Every data project has the same structure.

Once I realized this, building got much faster.

The Universal Data Pipeline:

Stage 1: Ingestion
- Accept input (CSV, API, scrape)
- Validate format
- Log raw data

Stage 2: Cleaning
- Standardize formats
- Handle missing values
- Remove duplicates
- Apply transformations

Stage 3: Enhancement
- AI classification/categorization
- Entity extraction
- Pattern detection

Stage 4: Storage
- Structured database
- Search indexes
- Checkpoints for recovery

Stage 5: Output
- Multiple export formats
- API access
- Dashboard views

Why this works:

Every project fits this pattern:

- Job classifier: Upload CSV -> Clean -> Classify -> Export
- Content aggregator: Scrape RSS -> Clean -> Analyze -> Store
- Vendor tool: Search -> Extract -> Enrich -> Export

The implementation pattern:

/project
├── /ingestion    # Data input handling
├── /cleaning     # Transformation rules
├── /enhancement  # AI processing
├── /storage      # Database layer
├── /output       # Export/API
├── /config       # Rules and settings
└── /checkpoints  # Recovery data

Key features I always include:

1. Checkpointing - Save state every N rows. Resume from failure.
2. Audit trail - Log every transformation. Know what happened to each row.
3. Selective reprocessing - Fix specific rows without rerunning everything.

How to apply this:

1. Start with the structure above
2. Fill in each stage for your specific project
3. Copy the pattern to your next project
4. Refine over time

Takeaway: First project: Built from scratch. Took a week. Now: Copy the pattern. Customize. Done in hours.

posts.title: The moment I realized I could actually build things
posts.body:
It wasn't when my first project worked.

It was when my first project failed and I fixed it.

The story:

I asked: 'Build me a job listing scraper.'

Got code. Ran it. Crashed immediately.

The old me would have:
- Concluded 'I can't do this'
- Given up
- Hired someone

What I did instead:

Copied the error message.
Pasted it back to Claude.

'I got this error: [error]'

Claude: 'Ah, you need to install this library. Run pip install requests.'

Ran it again. Different error.
Pasted that too.

The back-and-forth:

- Error #1: Missing library -> Fixed (pip install)
- Error #2: Wrong URL format -> Fixed (added https://)
- Error #3: HTML structure changed -> Fixed (updated selector)

posts.title: The selective reprocessing pattern that saves hours of data work
posts.body:
You've processed 50,000 rows.

Then you realize 500 of them need different handling.

Old way: Rerun everything (4 hours).

New way: Selective reprocessing (5 minutes).

The Pattern:

Core principle: Never reprocess what's already correct.

Implementation:

1. Tag every row with processing status
- processed
- needs_review
- failed
- reprocess_needed

2. Store the rules applied
- Which transformation ran
- When it ran
- What version of rules

3. Enable filtering for reprocessing
- By status
- By rule version
- By specific criteria

Example:

Job listings dataset.

Original processing: Basic categorization.

Problem: 'Aircraft maintenance' was categorized as generic 'Technician.'

Solution:
- Filter: WHERE title CONTAINS 'aircraft'
- Apply: New rule for Aviation Mechanic category
- Save: Update only those 500 rows

The time savings:

Rerun everything: 4 hours
Selective reprocess: 5 minutes

How to implement:

1. Add a 'processing_status' column to your data
2. Add a 'rule_version' column
3. Log original and processed values
4. Build a 'reprocess' function that filters before running

The architecture:

processing_log table:
- row_id
- rule_id
- rule_version
- status
- processed_at
- original_value
- processed_value

Takeaway: Real data projects are iterative. Rules evolve. Edge cases appear. Requirements change. Build for iteration from day one. Assume rules will change. Design for surgical updates.

posts.title: The prompting patterns that work (after 26 projects)
tweets:
The prompting patterns that work (after 26 projects).

Not theory. Tested approaches.

Here are the patterns I use every day:

Pattern #1: Problem-First

❌ 'Build me a scraper'

✓ 'I need to collect contact info from business websites. Input: list of URLs. Output: CSV with name, email, phone.'

Start with the problem, not the solution.

Pattern #2: Simplest First

❌ 'Build a full-featured dashboard with...'

✓ 'What's the simplest version of this that would be useful? Let's start there.'

Always ask for MVP first.

Pattern #3: Context Reference

❌ Re-explaining everything every time.

✓ 'Looking at my CLAUDE.md, let's add [feature] to the existing [component].'

Assume Claude has your context (if you've set it up).

Pattern #4: Error Sharing

❌ 'It's not working.'

✓ 'I got this error: [full error message including stack trace]'

Share exact errors. Always. The full thing.

Pattern #5: Constraints First

❌ 'Make it better.'

✓ 'It needs to: handle 10K+ rows, complete in under 5 minutes, export to CSV.'

Specify constraints before asking for solutions.

Pattern #6: Examples Over Descriptions

❌ 'Parse job titles correctly.'

✓ 'Parse these examples: \'HVAC Tech - Great Benefits\' should become \'HVAC Technician\'. \'Blair Stone Location Hiring\' should become \'Unknown\'.'

Show, don't tell.

Pattern #7: Iteration Acceptance

❌ 'This should work perfectly the first time.'

✓ 'Let's iterate on this. Run it and see what happens.'

Plan for 3-5 iterations. That's normal.

Pattern #8: Specific Feedback

❌ 'Make it better.'

✓ 'The output is missing [X]. Add [Y] to handle cases where [Z].'

Directional feedback works. Vague feedback doesn't.

Takeaway: Clarity compounds.

The clearer you are, the better Claude performs.
The better Claude performs, the faster you ship.

Specific > vague. Small steps > big leaps. Examples > descriptions.

My Voice Documentation System:

- Colloquialisms you use
- Industry terms you prefer
- Phrases unique to you
- Words you never use

Example from mine: 'thick skinned,' 'ahead of their skis,' 'burns from zero to one'

Section 2: Grammar Patterns

Document your quirks:
- Do you start sentences with 'And' or 'But'? (I do)
- Sentence fragments or complete sentences? (Both)
- Active or passive voice? (Active always)
- Short sentences or long? (Mix, but lean short)

Section 3: Punctuation Style

Yes, this matters:
- Dashes for emphasis? (I use them constantly)
- Ellipses for trailing off? (Sometimes...)
- Exclamation points frequency? (Sparingly)

Section 4: Content Patterns

How you structure ideas:
- Lists or paragraphs? (Lots of lists)
- Story-first or insight-first? (Insight, then story)
- How you open posts? (Hook, then context)
- How you close posts? (Takeaway, then CTA)

Section 5: Examples

Most important:
- 10+ examples of your best writing
- Annotated to explain what makes them 'you'
- Cover different content types

How to build this:

1. Review your last 20 posts
2. Note patterns you see
3. Document specific examples
4. Add to a Voice Profile file
5. Reference in every content prompt

Takeaway: Before: Generic AI content that could be anyone. After: Content that sounds like me because it's trained on how I actually write. Specificity wins.

posts.title: The token-efficient architecture that makes my AI actually useful
posts.body:
Most people overload AI with context.

Everything. All at once.

Result: Confused, generic outputs.

I built a system that loads only what's relevant.

The Token-Efficient Architecture:

Problem:

AI context windows have limits. Loading everything = wasted tokens + confused responses.

Solution:

Modular context loading.

How it works:

1. Context Categories

My Personal OS has separate context modules:
- Professional profile (resume, skills, goals)
- Communication style (voice documentation)
- Project information (CLAUDE.md files)
- Content frameworks (hook patterns, templates)

2. Session-Based Loading

Working on content? Load:
- Voice profile
- Content frameworks
- Recent project updates

Working on a specific project? Load:
- That project's CLAUDE.md
- Related tech decisions
- Current blockers

3. Hierarchical Structure

Summary level: Always loaded (50 tokens)
Detail level: Loaded on demand (500+ tokens)

'Tell me about my writing style' -> Loads detailed voice profile
'What should I work on?' -> Loads project summaries only

How to implement:

1. Split your context into categories
2. Create summary and detail versions of each
3. Load summaries by default
4. Load details when specific category is referenced

The Results:

- Faster responses (less to process)
- More relevant outputs (focused context)
- Lower costs (fewer tokens)
- Better quality (AI not confused by irrelevant info)

Takeaway: Context quality > context quantity. The right information, loaded at the right time, beats information overload every time.
